title: As temperatures get hotter, pesticides are more dangerous to farmworkers
gist: A growing body of research finds rising temperatures amplify pesticide harms to the US's 2.4 million farmworkers—by increasing exposure, toxicity, and use—while federal and state heat protections remain weak or actively banned in states like Florida and Texas.

insights.claim: Heat makes the body more vulnerable to pesticides, increases evaporation and thus airborne exposure, and boosts chemical transformation of pesticides into more toxic compounds, while protective PVC gloves break down at higher temperatures.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: Climate change compounds occupational chemical risk—relevant to agricultural labor cost, litigation exposure, and pesticide regulation.

insights.claim: Rising temperatures are expected to expand pesticide use as pests, pathogens, and weeds enlarge their ranges.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: A warming-driven tailwind for agrochemical demand, with offsetting regulatory and health-liability risk.

insights.claim: OSHA proposed a heat-hazard workplace standard in 2024 that is moving forward only slowly, leaving reliance on the general duty clause of the 1970 OSH Act.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: Regulatory uncertainty on heat standards affects agriculture and construction labor compliance costs.
insights.locator: There are few federal or state regulatory protections

insights.claim: Seven states have heat protections while Florida and Texas ban local governments from enacting them; Florida's 2024 law preempted a Miami-Dade proposal requiring water and rest breaks above a 95-degree heat index.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: Sharp state-level policy divergence creates uneven labor-cost and liability landscapes for agricultural employers.

insights.claim: A majority of US farmworkers were born abroad and are people of color, with field workers who never directly handle chemicals accounting for the majority of reported poisonings, and chronic exposure linked to cancer, diabetes, and neurodegenerative disease.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: Frames a labor-justice and immigration-linked vulnerability that shapes agricultural workforce stability.
insights.quote: This is definitely a case of environmental injustice
